bib.title: Foundations of Bayesian Learning (Chapter 34, Bandit Algorithms)

question: How should uncertainty over the environment be represented and updated (priors, posteriors, conjugacy) and how is regret defined from the Bayesian viewpoint, as groundwork for Bayesian bandits and Thompson sampling?
contributions: Statistical decision theory framing: dominated, admissible, minimax and Bayes optimal policies
Posterior definition with measure-theoretic rigour and the non-uniqueness issue
Conjugate pairs: Gaussian/Gaussian, Bernoulli/Beta, exponential families
Bayesian bandit environment, posterior in bandits, Bayesian regret

results.claim: Bayesian regret is the regret integrated over the prior; a bound on it does not generally imply a bound on frequentist regret, while a pointwise bound Rn<=f(nu) gives BRn<=E[f(nu)].
results.setup: k-armed Bayesian bandit (E,G,Q,P), n rounds; Note 2
results.quote:
The Bayesian regret of an algorithm is less informative than the frequentist
regret.

results.claim: Bayesian optimal policy minimises expected loss under the prior; the Bayesian optimal policy for regret equals the reward-maximising policy, but need not exist (an eps-optimal policy always does).
results.quote:
Note that the regret-minimising policy is the same as the reward-maximising
policy

results.claim: Even the Bayesian optimal policy can have strictly positive Bayesian regret (it cannot know the best arm from round one).
results.setup: Exercise 34.8 hint, prior over finite-armed bandits rich enough
results.quote:
the Bayesian regret of the Bayesian optimal policy
can be strictly greater
than zero

results.claim: Marble example: prior P(ww)=1/2, P(wb)=1/2; after observing one white marble the posterior P(ww|ow) is 2/3.
results.setup: Bag of two marbles, ww or wb, one drawn blindly

results.claim: Gaussian prior N(mu_P,sigma_P^2) with Gaussian model variance sigma_S^2: posterior mean is precision-weighted average of prior mean and observation; posterior variance (1/sigma_S^2+1/sigma_P^2)^-1.
results.setup: Section 34.3, one observation x, known signal variance

results.claim: Bernoulli model with Beta(alpha,beta) prior: after observing x in {0,1} the posterior is Beta(alpha+x, beta+1-x); after t observations Beta(alpha+S_t, beta+t-S_t).
Predictive probability of success after t Bernoulli observations under Beta(alpha,beta) is (alpha+S_t)/(alpha+beta+t) (the posterior mean).
Exponential-family conjugate prior with parameters (x0,n0) updates to ((n0*x0+x)/(n0+1), n0+1) after one observation x; n0 acts as a pseudo-count.
Bernoulli prior from exponential-family form equals Beta with alpha=1+n0*x0, beta=1+n0*(1-x0).
Gaussian prior N(mu,sigma^2), unit-variance Gaussian model: posterior N(mu_t,sigma_t^2) with mu_t=(mu/sigma^2+S_t)/(1/sigma^2+t), sigma_t^2=(1/sigma^2+t)^-1.
results.quote: Let (Θ, G) = (R, B(R)) and Q = N(µ, σ2)

results.claim: Bayesian Bernoulli bandit with product Beta prior has a posterior that is a product of Betas, each arm updated with its own successes s_i and pulls t_i: exponents alpha+s_i-1 and beta+t_i-s_i-1.
results.quote:
the
posterior is also the product of Beta distributions, each updated according to the
observations from the relevant arm.

results.claim: Exponential weights with learning rate 1 is the Bayesian posterior over experts; with uniform prior over k experts the log-loss regret is at most log k for every sequence.
results.setup: Note 5, prediction with expert advice under logarithmic loss; exercise 34.6
results.quote:
the regret is bounded
by Rn ≤log(k) for all sequences y1, . . . , yn.

results.claim: Ridge regression estimator is the posterior mean under a Gaussian model with known variance and a zero-mean Gaussian prior with covariance I/lambda.
results.quote: is the mean of the Bayesian posterior when the model is Gaussian with known variance

results.claim: In classical settings all Bayes optimal policies (unique ones) are admissible and admissible policies are Bayes optimal for some prior or limit of such; for stochastic Bernoulli bandits every admissible policy is Bayes optimal for some prior (Ex 34.15).
results.quote:
all admissible policies
for stochastic
Bernoulli bandits are Bayesian optimal for some prior

limits: Sections 34.2.1 (rigorous posterior), Theorem 34.1, Example 34.2, 34.3.1 (exponential family measure theory), 34.3.2 Markov chain view, and Notes 7-9 are measure-theoretic background; the authors say readers familiar with it can skim Sec 34.4 and 34.6 for notation only.
No algorithm or empirical result in the chapter; no Thompson sampling or Bayesian regret bound (those are chapters 35 and 36).
Authors concede a bound on Bayesian regret does not give a bound on frequentist regret (Note 2) and that the exponential-weights analogy should not be taken too seriously (Note 5).
Authors say they know of no practical situation where the non-unique posterior goes awry (Note 7).
practices: Prefer comparing problem definitions and solution methods over Bayesian-versus-frequentist labels (Sec 34.1).
Choose a prior for which the posterior can be computed or sampled efficiently, not only one that encodes belief (Sec 34.3).
Analyse the frequentist regret of Bayesian algorithms, since Bayesian regret is less informative (Note 2).
When using Bayesian posteriors inside a frequentist argument, state which version of the posterior is used (Sec 34.2.1).
Treat bandit algorithm design as designing policy schema evaluated across many problem classes (Note 4).
